title: Brand Strategy & Positioning
subtitle: Research a market, choose a target and write a positioning strategy that helps a business win customers without fighting on price, then offer this work to paying clients.
description: An advanced, practical course in the thinking behind strong brands. You will segment and target a market, use customer interviews, competitor audits and perceptual maps to find a real point of difference, test positioning routes, and turn the result into a short brand guideline. The final module shows you how to run discovery, price and propose positioning projects, lead workshops and report results honestly.
outcomes: Write a positioning statement backed by customer and competitor evidence
Segment a market and choose a primary target with a weighted scoring table
Run customer interviews, review mining, a competitor audit and a perceptual map
Test positioning routes with customers and turn the winner into a messaging house and mini brand guideline
Price, propose and scope a positioning project and lead a team workshop
Measure brand health after launch and present results in an honest case study
audience: Women who already understand basic marketing or run a business and want to set clear brand direction for their own business or offer positioning work to clients.
tools: Canva (free plan) for maps and route cards

modules.title: Brand Strategy Foundations: Brand, Position and Target
modules.overview: Learn exactly what a brand strategy decides, the professional vocabulary of positioning, and how to choose the customer segment you will compete for. You finish the module with three draft positioning statements and a scored target segment.

lessons.title: Brand, identity and positioning: what a brand strategy actually decides
objectives: Explain the difference between a brand, a brand identity and a brand position
Describe the five decisions every brand strategy must make
Show with simple numbers why a business with no clear position gets pulled into price fights
Run a quick three-word brand perception check with real customers

blocks.text: People often say "brand" when they mean the logo. In strategy work we separate three ideas. Your **brand** is what people think and feel when they hear the business name: the memories, opinions and expectations stored in their heads. Your **brand identity** is the set of tools you control that trigger those memories: the name, logo, colours, packaging, photos and the way you write. Your **brand position** is the specific place you want to own in the customer's mind, compared with the other choices she has.

The word positioning was made popular by two American advertising men, **Al Ries and Jack Trout**, first in trade magazine articles and then in their 1981 book *Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind*. Their key point still holds: positioning is not what you do to a product, it is what you do to the mind of the buyer. You cannot add a position by printing a new flyer. You earn it by choosing a clear idea and repeating it, in words and in actions, until customers connect that idea with you.

blocks.name: stand-out
blocks.alt: A person standing apart from a crowd of similar figures
blocks.caption: A clear position is how one business stands out among many that sell almost the same thing.

blocks.text: Five decisions inside every brand strategy
A brand strategy is a short set of decisions, written down, that guide everything the business says and does. Whatever template you use, it has to answer these five questions:

head: Decision
Question it answers
Weak answer
Strong answer
rows: Office admins in Port Harcourt who order snacks for meetings
What will she compare us with?
Other small chops vendors and supermarket snack trays
Why choose us over those options?
Delivered hot, on the agreed time, with a proper invoice
On-time delivery log, sample invoice, repeat office clients
How do we sound and behave?

blocks.text: Notice that the weak answers are not wrong, they are just useless. "Quality and good service" is what every competitor also says, so it cannot help a customer choose. A strong answer is narrow enough that some customers will say "this is not for me". That is a good sign. A position that tries to please everybody ends up meaning nothing to anybody.

blocks.title: Layers of a brand strategy
items: Purpose: why we exist
Positioning: who and against what
Promise and proof
Personality and voice
Identity and touchpoints
blocks.caption: Each layer rests on the one above it: logos and posts come last, after the thinking is done.

blocks.text: Start with why, then be specific

Simon Sinek's well known TED talk describes the **Golden Circle**: why you do it, how you do it, and what you sell. Most businesses describe only the what ("we sell small chops"). Purpose gives a brand energy, but purpose alone is not positioning. "We want to make people happy" is a purpose many brands share. Positioning turns purpose into a specific, testable choice about a customer, an alternative and a difference.
Why unclear brands end up fighting on price

When customers see no real difference between sellers, the only thing left to compare is price. The seller then has to match every discount, and profit disappears quickly because discounts come straight out of profit, not out of costs.

blocks.title: Worked example: two small chops vendors, same cost
blocks.context: For example, Ada and Bisi both run small chops businesses in Port Harcourt. Each 100-piece office tray costs them about 60,000 naira (approximate) in ingredients, packaging, gas and transport.
steps: Ada has no clear position. She sells at 75,000 naira. Profit per tray: 75,000 minus 60,000 = 15,000 naira.
A customer says another vendor is cheaper, so Ada gives 10% off: 10% of 75,000 = 7,500 naira. Her profit falls to 15,000 minus 7,500 = 7,500 naira. One discount halved her profit.

Bisi positions herself for office admins: hot delivery at the agreed time, a proper invoice and receipt, and a named contact who answers. She sells at 95,000 naira. Profit: 95,000 minus 60,000 = 35,000 naira.
Admins who have been embarrassed by late food before are happy to pay more for reliability, so Bisi rarely gets asked for a discount.
blocks.result: With the same costs, Bisi earns 35,000 naira per tray while Ada, after one discount, earns 7,500 naira. The difference is not the recipe, it is a clear, believable position for a specific buyer.

blocks.title: A position must be true
blocks.text: Never promise what the business cannot deliver every time. A broken promise damages the brand faster than having no promise. In Nigeria, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) protects consumers against misleading claims, and advertising is regulated by the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON). Build your position on things you can prove.
Common mistakes to avoid

items: Treating a new logo as a new strategy. Identity should express a position, not replace it.
Choosing a target of "everyone". Even large brands choose a core customer first.
Copying the leader's message. If the leader owns "cheapest", saying "cheapest" louder rarely works.
Forgetting that "do nothing" and "do it myself" are competitors too. A home cook is an alternative to a caterer.

blocks.text: Throughout this course you will build one complete **Brand Positioning Strategy Package** for a real or practice business. Pick that business now: your own, a friend's, or a small business you buy from often. Each lesson's activity adds one piece to it.

takeaways: A brand lives in customers' minds; identity is the tools you control; positioning is the place you choose to own.
Every strategy decides target, frame of reference, difference, proof and personality.
Narrow, true and provable beats broad and vague.
Without a clear difference, customers compare price only, and discounts eat profit fast.

activity.title: Three-word brand perception check
steps: Choose the business you will use for this whole course and write its name and what it sells.
Ask the owner (or yourself) to write three words they want customers to think of.
Message five real customers on WhatsApp: 'What three words come to mind when you think of [business]?'
Put the owner's words and the customers' words side by side and circle any that match.
Write two sentences on the gap between the intended brand and the real brand.
activity.evidence: A note or photo of the side-by-side word lists and your two-sentence gap summary.

lessons.title: The positioning toolkit: segments, points of difference and the positioning statement
objectives: Define target segment, frame of reference, points of parity, points of difference and reason to believe
Write a positioning statement using the standard template
Test a point of difference against three questions: relevant, distinctive, deliverable
Describe a brand personality using Aaker's five dimensions

blocks.text: Professional brand strategists use a small, precise vocabulary. Learn these terms well, because clients, agencies and marketing teams use them in briefs and meetings, and because each term forces a decision.

head: Term
Plain meaning
rows: The specific group of customers you are built for, described by needs and situation, not only age and location
The category or set of alternatives the customer compares you with
The basics you must match so you are not rejected (for example, clean kitchen, fair price range)
The few things you do better or differently that the target truly values
The proof that makes your difference credible
The full bundle of benefits a customer gets for the price she pays
A short, consistent commitment the customer can expect every time

blocks.name: target-audience
blocks.alt: A target with people icons around it
blocks.caption: Positioning starts by choosing a specific target segment, not 'everyone'.

blocks.text: Parity first, then difference

Kevin Lane Keller, Brian Sternthal and Alice Tybout explained in a 2002 Harvard Business Review article that strong positioning needs both **points of parity** and **points of difference** within a clear **frame of reference**. Parity gets you onto the shortlist. Difference wins the choice. A hair salon that offers a unique style but keeps customers waiting three hours has a difference but fails on parity, so customers leave anyway.

A good point of difference passes three tests. It is **relevant**: the target segment actually cares. It is **distinctive**: competitors do not already own it. It is **deliverable**: the business can keep it true every week, not just during a launch. If a difference fails any one test, drop it or fix the operation behind it first.
The positioning statement

A positioning statement is an internal sentence, not an advert. It guides decisions about products, prices, photos and posts. A widely used template, popularised by Geoffrey Moore in the technology world, is:

blocks.title: Parts of a positioning statement
items: For (target segment)
Who (need or problem)
Our brand is (category)
That (key benefit)
Unlike (main alternative)
Because (reason to believe)
blocks.caption: Read left to right: each part narrows the idea until it can guide real decisions.

blocks.title: Worked example: positioning a tutoring centre in Abuja
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa runs a small after-school tutoring centre in Gwarinpa, Abuja. Her first draft said: 'We offer quality education for all children.'
steps: Target: she checks her records. Most paying parents have children in JSS3 or SS3 preparing for BECE, WAEC or NECO, and both parents work full time.
Need: these parents worry about exam results but cannot supervise homework on weekdays.
Frame of reference: home lesson teachers and larger tutorial centres.
Points of parity: qualified tutors, safe premises, fees in the normal range for the area.
Point of difference she can deliver: a short WhatsApp progress report to each parent every Friday, with the topics covered and one score.
Reason to believe: sample reports (with names hidden) and her published weekly schedule.
blocks.result: Her statement: 'For working parents in Gwarinpa whose children are preparing for BECE or WAEC, Hauwa's Study Hub is an exam-focused tutoring centre that keeps you informed every week. Unlike home lesson teachers, we send a written progress report every Friday, so you always know where your child stands.'

blocks.text: Before you keep any statement, run the **swap test**. Replace your brand name with a competitor's name and read the statement again. If it still sounds true for the competitor, your point of difference is not really different, and customers will not be able to tell you apart either. Hauwa's statement passes, because no nearby centre sends a weekly written report. A statement like 'quality tutoring with caring teachers' fails, because every centre in Abuja could say it.

blocks.title: Write three, keep one
blocks.text: Draft three different statements built on three different points of difference, then test them with real customers (you will learn how in Module 2). The first idea is rarely the strongest.
Brand personality

Personality describes how the brand behaves and sounds, as if it were a person. Researcher Jennifer Aaker identified five broad dimensions of brand personality: **sincerity** (honest, warm), **excitement** (daring, lively), **competence** (reliable, intelligent), **sophistication** (refined, upper class) and **ruggedness** (tough, outdoorsy). Most brands lead with one or two. Hauwa's centre should lead with competence and sincerity. A party DJ brand would lead with excitement.

items: Pick one or two dimensions, not all five.
Turn each into behaviour: for competence, 'we reply within two hours and never miss a report'.
Check that the personality fits the target: busy parents want calm and reliable, not loud and trendy.

blocks.title: Statement versus tagline
blocks.text: The positioning statement is long and internal. A tagline is a short public line that may come from it later. Hauwa's tagline might become 'Know where your child stands, every Friday.' Never publish the raw statement as your slogan.

takeaways: Parity gets you considered; difference gets you chosen.
A point of difference must be relevant, distinctive and deliverable.
The positioning statement names target, need, category, benefit, alternative and proof.
Personality is shown through behaviour, not adjectives alone.

activity.title: Draft three positioning statements
steps: List the points of parity your course business must meet (at least four).
List three possible points of difference and score each one yes or no for relevant, distinctive and deliverable.
Write three positioning statements using the six-part template, one for each difference.
Choose one or two Aaker personality dimensions and write two behaviours for each.
Save the three statements for testing in Module 2.
activity.evidence: A one-page note with your parity list, difference scores, three statements and personality behaviours.

lessons.title: Choosing where to compete: segmenting and targeting in African markets
objectives: Segment a market by needs, occasions, price tier and channel
Score segments with a simple weighted table and choose a primary target
Explain how informal trade, WhatsApp selling and diaspora buyers change targeting decisions
Check a segment against the five tests of a useful segment

blocks.text: Positioning only works once you know whose mind you are trying to win. Marketers call the full process **segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP)**: split the market into groups with different needs, choose the group you will serve best, then position for that group. Lesson 2 gave you the positioning tools. This lesson is about the choice that comes before them.

blocks.name: segmentation
blocks.alt: Groups of people sorted into different coloured clusters
blocks.caption: Segmentation splits one market into groups with different needs, so you can choose where to compete.

blocks.text: Four ways to split a market

head: Basis
What you look at
Example for a shea butter brand
rows: The problem or job the buyer is solving
Dry skin relief, baby skin care, hair growth routine
When and why the purchase happens
Daily use, gifts, wedding favours, travel
How much the buyer expects to pay and why
Open market loose butter, mid-range branded tubs, premium gift jars
Open market, pharmacy shelf, WhatsApp vendor, Jumia, diaspora order

blocks.text: Age, gender and location (demographics) still matter, but needs and occasions usually explain buying better. Two 30-year-old women in Kano may buy the same product for completely different reasons, one for her own skin and one as a wedding gift. Each reason needs a different message and package.
What makes a segment worth choosing

blocks.title: Five tests of a useful segment
items: Measurable: you can estimate size
Substantial: big enough to pay
Reachable: you can get to them
Different: they respond differently
Actionable: you can serve them
blocks.caption: If a segment fails any test, it is an idea, not a target.

blocks.text: These five tests are a long-standing checklist in marketing textbooks. In African markets, **reachable** deserves extra attention. Can you reach the segment through channels you can afford: WhatsApp groups, church or mosque networks, market associations, Instagram, local radio, or a pharmacy owner who trusts you? A segment you cannot reach cheaply is not your segment yet.
Score your options with numbers

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a target for a shea butter brand
blocks.context: For example, Zainab processes clean, filtered shea butter near Tamale and sells it across Ghana and to Nigerian buyers online. She compares three segments using four criteria, each scored 1 (poor) to 5 (strong), with weights she agrees with her sister.
steps: Weights: size 30%, willingness to pay 30%, reachability 25%, fit with her strengths 15%.
Segment A, mothers buying for babies: size 4, pay 3, reach 4, fit 5. Score = 4x0.30 + 3x0.30 + 4x0.25 + 5x0.15 = 1.20 + 0.90 + 1.00 + 0.75 = 3.85.
Segment B, wedding favour planners: size 2, pay 5, reach 3, fit 3. Score = 0.60 + 1.50 + 0.75 + 0.45 = 3.30.
Segment C, diaspora natural hair buyers: size 3, pay 5, reach 2, fit 4. Score = 0.90 + 1.50 + 0.50 + 0.60 = 3.50.
She checks that her weights add up: 30 + 30 + 25 + 15 = 100%.
blocks.result: Segment A wins with 3.85, so Zainab positions first for mothers who want a gentle, clean product for babies. She keeps Segment C as a second target for later, once she has a reliable shipping partner.

blocks.title: Health claims need care
blocks.text: When a segment is about babies, skin or health, never claim the product treats or cures a condition unless you have proper approval. In Nigeria, cosmetics and similar products must meet NAFDAC requirements, and claims on labels and adverts must be honest. Position on things like clean processing and gentle use, which you can show, rather than medical benefits.
African market realities that change targeting

items: **Informal and formal side by side.** The same customer may buy loose products in the open market and branded ones online. Decide which buying moment you are targeting.
**Trust travels through people.** Referrals in WhatsApp groups, religious communities and associations often matter more than adverts. Target segments where you already have trusted links.
**Price sensitivity is real but not universal.** Many buyers trade down when prices rise, but some segments, such as gift buyers or busy professionals, still pay for convenience and reliability.
**Diaspora buyers** in the UK, US and elsewhere often want home products they trust, but shipping, customs rules and payment options must be solved before you target them.
**Mobile first.** Most of your target will see your brand on a phone screen first, so your position must be clear in a WhatsApp profile or an Instagram bio of a few lines.

blocks.text: A strong brand often starts narrow and widens later. Owning one segment well gives you referrals, testimonials and cash, which pay for the next segment. Trying to serve five segments at once usually means five half-finished messages and confused customers.

Check your choice with the people who will carry it out. If the owner, staff or rider dislike serving the chosen segment, the position will slowly fade in daily practice. Zainab's team, for example, enjoys explaining gentle use to new mothers, which makes the baby care segment easier to keep.

blocks.title: One primary, one secondary
blocks.text: Write down one primary segment that gets most of your effort and money, and at most one secondary segment. Everything else goes on a 'later' list.

takeaways: STP means segment, target, then position, in that order.
Needs and occasions usually explain buying better than age and location alone.
A useful segment is measurable, substantial, reachable, different and actionable.
Weighted scoring turns a gut feeling into a decision you can explain to a client.

activity.title: Segment scoring sheet
steps: List three to four possible segments for your course business using needs, occasions, price tier or channel.
Agree four criteria and weights that add up to 100%.
Score each segment 1 to 5 on each criterion and calculate the weighted totals.
Check the winner against the five tests of a useful segment.
Name one primary and one secondary segment and update your best positioning statement from Lesson 2.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your scoring table with the calculations and your chosen primary segment.

quiz.q: Two vendors have the same costs. One is clearly positioned for a specific buyer and rarely discounts; the other matches every discount. What is the main lesson?
options: A clear, believable position protects price and profit
The cheaper vendor will always win in the long run
Positioning only matters for large companies
Discounts increase profit because volume always rises
quiz.explain: When customers see a real difference that matters to them, they compare more than price, so the business does not need to give away its profit.

quiz.q: A salon is famous for creative styles, but customers wait three hours and leave. In positioning terms, what is failing?
quiz.explain: Waiting time is a basic expectation. Failing a point of parity removes the brand from consideration, even with a strong difference.

quiz.q: Which point of difference passes all three tests: relevant, distinctive and deliverable?
options: 'We offer quality service' when every competitor says the same
'We deliver within one hour' when the owner has no rider
'A written progress report every Friday' that parents value and no local competitor offers
'We are the best in Nigeria' with no proof
quiz.explain: It matters to the target, competitors do not own it, and the business can keep doing it every week.

quiz.q: A segment scores size 4, pay 2, reach 5, fit 3 with weights 30%, 30%, 25%, 15%. What is its weighted score?
Which statement best describes a positioning statement?
options: A public slogan printed on every flyer
An internal sentence that names target, need, category, benefit, alternative and proof
A list of the owner's favourite colours
A legal registration of the brand name
quiz.explain: The statement is a decision tool for the team. A tagline may later come from it, but the two are different.

quiz.q: A skincare maker wants to target mothers buying for babies. Which message is the safest and strongest position?
options: 'Clean, filtered shea butter, gently processed, with nothing added'
'Doctors everywhere recommend us' without any evidence
quiz.explain: It is relevant to the segment and can be shown. Medical cure claims and invented endorsements are misleading and can break consumer protection and NAFDAC rules.

modules.title: Research, Workflow and Brand Guidelines
modules.overview: Use free tools to research customers and competitors, run a structured four-week positioning project, test positioning routes with real customers, and turn the winning route into a short brand guideline with quality checks.

lessons.title: Research tools: customer interviews, review mining, competitor audits and perceptual maps
objectives: Run a short customer interview that uncovers the real 'job' a customer hires a product to do
Mine online reviews and comments for the exact words customers use
Build a competitor audit grid and a two-axis perceptual map
Collect and store research data with consent, following basic data protection practice

blocks.text: Brand strategy is built on evidence, not on the owner's opinion. The good news is that the core tools are free and work on a smartphone: WhatsApp, Google Forms, Google Sheets, Google Maps reviews, Instagram and a notebook. What makes them professional is how you use them.

blocks.name: marketing-analysis
blocks.alt: A person reviewing charts and marketing data on a screen
blocks.caption: Research turns guesses about customers and competitors into evidence you can show a client.

blocks.text: Tool 1: the customer interview

Talk to real buyers, one at a time, by phone, video call or in person. A practical starting point is five to eight people from your primary segment. Stop when you keep hearing the same answers. Ask about **past behaviour**, not opinions about the future, because people are poor at predicting what they will do.

items: "Tell me about the last time you bought [product]. What was happening that day?"
"What else did you consider, including doing it yourself or not buying?"
"What almost stopped you from buying?"
"How would you describe this business to a friend?"
"What would make you stop using it?"

blocks.text: These questions follow the **jobs to be done** idea described by Clayton Christensen and colleagues in Harvard Business Review: customers "hire" a product to make progress in a particular situation. A working mother does not just buy laundry service. She hires it to get her Saturday back and to look neat at work on Monday. That job, not the product feature, is what your position must speak to.

Take notes in the customer's own words, not your summary of them. After each interview, write the three most important things you heard within the hour, while you still remember the tone. Never argue or explain your product during an interview; you are there to learn, not to sell. If someone criticises the business, thank them, because complaints often point straight to a point of parity that needs fixing.
Tool 2: review and comment mining

Open Google Maps reviews, Instagram comments, Facebook pages and Jumia or Konga reviews for your business and three competitors. Copy phrases customers repeat into a sheet with three columns: praise, complaint, exact words. Customers' own words often make the best taglines and captions later, because they sound natural to other customers.
Tool 3: the competitor audit grid

For each competitor record the same six things: who they seem to target, their main promise, price range, channels, tone of voice, and the proof they show. Look at their WhatsApp business profile, Instagram bio, signage and how they reply to a test enquiry. Keep the grid factual; you are mapping positions, not judging people.

Finally, make a test enquiry yourself, as a normal customer would. Note how fast each competitor replies, what they ask, and how they describe themselves. These small moments often reveal a competitor's real position better than their adverts do.
Tool 4: the perceptual map

A perceptual map places brands on two axes that customers actually care about, so you can see crowded areas and empty spaces. Choose the axes from your interviews and reviews, not from your own guesses. Price and quality are common, but speed, convenience, style or trust may matter more in your category.

blocks.title: Perceptual map: laundry services in Ibadan
items: Fast but expensive
Fast and affordable (gap)
Slow and expensive
Slow but cheap
blocks.caption: Most competitors cluster in two boxes; the empty box is a possible position if the business can deliver it.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding a gap in the laundry market
blocks.context: For example, Tolu runs a two-person laundry in Bodija, Ibadan, and wants a sharper position. She audits four competitors and interviews six customers.
steps: Audit: two hotel-linked dry cleaners charge about 1,500 naira (approximate) per shirt and return in 24 hours. Two neighbourhood washers charge about 400 naira per shirt but take five to seven days.
Interviews: five of six customers mention ironed work shirts ready for Monday as the real need. Four mention fear of lost items.
Reviews: competitors' complaints repeat the words 'lost my shirt' and 'they kept shifting the date'.
Map: nobody occupies 'affordable and fast'. Tolu checks her capacity: with pickup on Friday evening and return on Sunday evening she can handle about 40 shirts a week.
She prices at 700 naira per shirt with a tagged-item list sent on WhatsApp at pickup.
blocks.result: Tolu's position: weekend work-shirt service for young professionals, back by Sunday night, every item listed and tagged. It comes straight from customer words and an empty space on the map, and it is something she can deliver.

blocks.title: Respect customers' data
blocks.text: Ask permission before recording a call, tell people how you will use their answers, and do not share names, phone numbers or screenshots outside the project. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. When in doubt, store answers without names (Customer 1, Customer 2) and delete raw recordings after the project.

blocks.title: Use a free survey for numbers
blocks.text: Interviews give you depth. A short Google Form sent to a WhatsApp customer list can then check how common an answer is. Keep it under eight questions so people finish it on a phone.

takeaways: Interview about past behaviour, not future opinions.
Customers hire products to do a job in a situation; position on the job.
Review mining gives you the exact words customers use.
Choose perceptual map axes from customer evidence, then check you can deliver the gap.

activity.title: Research pack for your course business
steps: Interview at least five customers in your primary segment using the five questions, with their permission.
Mine reviews or comments for your business and three competitors and fill a praise, complaint, exact words sheet.
Complete a competitor audit grid with the six headings for at least three competitors.
Draw a perceptual map on paper or in Canva using two axes taken from your interviews.
Write three findings that surprised you.
activity.evidence: Your interview notes (without names), review sheet, competitor grid and a photo of your perceptual map.

lessons.title: From brief to delivery: running a four-week positioning project
objectives: Plan a positioning project in stages with hours and deliverables
Turn research notes into insight statements
Present two or three positioning routes and test them with customers
Read simple test results and recommend one route with reasons

blocks.text: Clients do not pay for frameworks. They pay for a clear decision they can act on. A good workflow gets you from a messy first conversation to that decision on time, with the client involved at the right moments so there are no surprises at the end.

blocks.name: design-process
blocks.alt: A person moving through connected steps of a process
blocks.caption: A visible process keeps the client involved and the project on schedule.

blocks.title: A four-week positioning project
items: Week 1: brief and discovery
Week 2: customer and competitor research
Week 3: insights and positioning routes
Week 4: testing, decision, handover
blocks.caption: Each week ends with something the client can see, so feedback comes early, not at the end.

blocks.text: Stage by stage

items: **Brief and kickoff.** Agree the business goal (for example, raise average order value or win office clients), the decision-maker, the budget, and what is out of scope. Write it in a one-page brief and get a 'yes' in writing.
**Discovery.** Interview the owner and one or two staff. Ask what the business does best, what customers praise, what they would never do, and where money is lost.
**Research.** Use the tools from Lesson 1: customer interviews, review mining, competitor grid, perceptual map.
**Synthesis.** Group findings and write insights. An insight has two parts: what you observed, and why it matters for the brand.
**Positioning routes.** Write two or three distinct routes. Each route has a target, a point of difference, a reason to believe and a sample tagline or WhatsApp bio.
**Testing and decision.** Show the routes to customers, count reactions, and recommend one route to the client with your reasons.
**Handover.** Deliver the strategy document and a short session showing staff how to use it.

blocks.text: Writing insights, not just findings

A finding is a fact: "Four of six customers mentioned lost items." An insight explains what it means: "Customers fear losing clothes more than they care about price, so visible tracking could be our strongest proof." Aim for five to seven insights. Each positioning route should be built on at least one of them.
Testing routes with real customers

Put each route on a simple card or WhatsApp image with the same layout so only the idea changes. Show the cards in a different order to each person, so the first card does not always win. Ask three questions: which one is most appealing to you, which one would you trust, and which one, if any, would make you willing to pay a little more.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading test results
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma is positioning a home cleaning service in Lekki. She tests three routes with 12 customers from her target segment of busy two-income households.
steps: Route A, 'Vetted, trained cleaners you can trust with your keys': chosen as most appealing by 7 of 12 people. 7 divided by 12 = 0.583, about 58%.
Route B, 'Spotless in three hours or we come back free': 3 of 12, which is 25%.
Route C, 'Eco-friendly cleaning products': 2 of 12, about 17%. Check: 7 + 3 + 2 = 12.
On 'which would you trust', Route A wins again with 8 of 12, about 67%.
Several people who chose Route B said they had been let down by guarantees before.
blocks.result: Ifeoma recommends Route A. She also notes that 12 people is a small sample, so the result guides the decision but does not prove it. She plans to track enquiries for three months after launch to confirm the route works.

blocks.text: Also listen to the reasons people give, not only their choice. A route that wins appeal but loses on trust may need stronger proof before launch. A route that nobody picks first but several people call 'believable' might become a supporting pillar later rather than the main promise.

blocks.title: Small samples, honest language
blocks.text: With 10 to 20 people you can see strong preferences, but do not present percentages as if they describe the whole market. Say '7 of the 12 customers we spoke to', not '58% of Lagos'.
Planning your hours

head: Stage
Typical hours for a small business
Deliverable the client sees
rows: Competitor grid, perceptual map, interview summary
Insight list and two or three route cards
Test results, final positioning and guideline

blocks.text: Adding the middle of each range gives about 6 + 10 + 7 + 7 = 30 hours. Use your own records after two or three projects to refine these numbers; they become the basis for your pricing in Module 3.

items: Keep all files in one shared Google Drive folder with sub-folders: 01 Brief, 02 Research, 03 Insights, 04 Routes, 05 Final.
Use Google Meet or a WhatsApp call for check-ins, and send a written summary after each one.
Name files with dates and versions, for example Positioning_Routes_v2_2026-10-12.

takeaways: A positioning project moves through brief, discovery, research, synthesis, routes, testing and handover.
Insights explain what a finding means for the brand.
Test routes with the same layout, shuffled order and the same three questions.
Report small samples honestly and confirm results after launch.

activity.title: Project plan and route cards
steps: Write a one-page brief for your course business: goal, decision-maker, scope, deadline.
Turn your Lesson 1 research into five insights using 'we saw, so it means'.
Write two or three positioning routes and design each as a simple card in Canva or on paper.
Show the cards to at least six target customers and record their answers to the three questions.
Calculate the share for each route and write your recommendation in three sentences.
activity.evidence: Your brief, insight list, route cards and a results table with your recommendation.

lessons.title: Brand guidelines, messaging and quality checks
objectives: Build a messaging house with a promise, three pillars and proof points
Write tone of voice rules and an elevator pitch that express the position
Run a consistency audit across a brand's touchpoints and score it
Document decisions with versions, sign-off and basic name protection checks

blocks.text: A positioning strategy only creates value when everyone uses it: the owner, staff, the designer, the person replying on WhatsApp. The brand guideline translates strategy into rules people can follow on a busy day. For a small business it can be five to eight pages, not a hundred.

blocks.name: reviewed-docs
blocks.alt: A person checking a set of approved documents
blocks.caption: A short, clear guideline turns strategy into rules the whole team can follow.

blocks.text: The messaging house

A messaging house is a simple structure used by many brand teams. The **roof** is the brand promise in one line. Under it stand **three pillars**, the main messages that support the promise. The **foundation** is the proof for each pillar: facts, processes, testimonials, numbers the business can show.

blocks.title: Worked example: a messaging house for Tolu's laundry
blocks.context: For example, Tolu from Lesson 1 has chosen the position 'weekend work-shirt service for young professionals, back by Sunday night, every item listed and tagged'.
steps: Roof (promise): 'Your work week starts neat. Every shirt back by Sunday night.'
Pillar 1, On time: Friday pickup, Sunday return. Proof: delivery log showing return times.
Pillar 2, Nothing lost: every item tagged and listed on WhatsApp at pickup. Proof: sample item list and tag photo.
Pillar 3, Work-ready finish: shirts pressed and hung, not folded. Proof: before and after photos with customer permission.
Elevator pitch: 'We collect your work shirts on Friday, tag and list every item, and return them pressed by Sunday night, so Monday morning is easy.'
blocks.result: Every caption, flyer, reply and price list now has a clear source. If a message does not support one of the three pillars, Tolu does not post it.

blocks.text: Tone of voice
Tone rules turn the personality chosen in Module 1 into words. The most useful format is a short 'we are, we are not' list with real examples of good and bad sentences.

blocks.title: Tolu's tone of voice
items: We are
We are not
blocks.caption: Pairs like these stop the brand sounding different every time a new person writes a post.

blocks.text: What goes in a small-business brand guideline

items: Positioning statement and target segment (one page).
Messaging house and elevator pitch.
Tone of voice rules with five example sentences.
Ready-to-copy text: WhatsApp Business description, Instagram bio, greeting and away messages, price list wording.
Visual direction: logo files and where they live, two or three brand colours with codes, photo style (for example, real shirts on hangers in daylight, no stock photos).
Do and do not examples, using screenshots.

blocks.text: Quality check: the consistency audit

Before handover, and again three months later, list every place a customer meets the brand and check each one against the guideline: does it state or support the promise, use the right tone, and show current prices and contacts?

Score it simply: if 6 of 10 touchpoints pass every check, consistency is 6 divided by 10 = 60%. Fix the easiest high-visibility items first, such as bios and greetings, then plan the costly ones, such as signage.
Making the guideline part of daily work

A guideline that sits in a folder changes nothing. Turn it into tools staff touch every day. Save the approved replies as **quick replies** in WhatsApp Business so anyone answering customers uses the same words. Keep logo files and colour codes in one shared folder and give the designer that link only. Print a one-page summary with the promise, the three pillars and the tone pairs and stick it where staff can see it. When a new person joins, spend fifteen minutes walking through that page with real examples of good and bad replies.

Write proof points as facts a customer could check, not adjectives. 'We are reliable' is a claim. 'Returned by Sunday night on 38 of our last 40 orders' is proof, as long as the log really shows it. Update proof points every few months so they stay true.
Documentation and sign-off

items: Keep a **decision log**: date, decision, who approved it, why. It prevents the same debate starting again next month.
Use version numbers and get written client sign-off on the final version, even by WhatsApp message.

Do a name check before finalising: search the CAC public search for business names and search social media and domains. Registering a business name with CAC is not the same as registering a trademark; trademarks in Nigeria go through the Trademarks, Patents and Designs Registry. Advise clients to consult a lawyer for trademark questions.

blocks.title: Do not use what you do not own
blocks.text: Guidelines should only include fonts, photos and icons the client has the right to use. Free tools like Canva have their own licence terms; check them before a brand relies on an element for its logo.

takeaways: A messaging house links one promise to three pillars and real proof.
Tone rules work best as 'we are, we are not' pairs with examples.
A small-business guideline should be short and ready to copy.
Audit touchpoints, score consistency and fix high-visibility items first.

activity.title: Mini brand guideline
steps: Build a messaging house for your course business: promise, three pillars, proof for each.
Write a 'we are, we are not' tone list with four pairs and five example sentences.
Write the WhatsApp Business description, Instagram bio and an elevator pitch.
Audit at least six touchpoints with the four-column table and calculate the consistency score.
Save everything as a five to eight page document named with a version number.
activity.evidence: Your mini brand guideline (PDF or Google Doc) and the scored audit table.

quiz.q: Which interview question is most useful for positioning research?
options: 'Would you buy this if we launched it next year?'
'Tell me about the last time you bought this. What was happening that day?'
'Don't you think we are better than the others?'
quiz.explain: Questions about real past behaviour reveal the job the customer was trying to get done. Future predictions and leading questions give unreliable answers.

quiz.q: Tolu's perceptual map shows no competitor in 'fast and affordable'. What should she do before claiming that position?
options: Claim it immediately on all channels
Check that her capacity and costs let her deliver it every week
Copy the most expensive competitor's message
quiz.explain: An empty space is only an opportunity if the business can deliver it reliably and profitably.

quiz.q: In a route test, 5 of 15 customers chose Route B. How should this be reported?
options: '33% of the market prefers Route B'
'5 of the 15 customers we spoke to, about 33%, chose Route B'
quiz.explain: 5 divided by 15 is about 33%. With a small sample, report the actual counts and avoid claiming it represents the whole market.

quiz.q: Which is an insight rather than a finding?
options: 'Four of six customers mentioned lost items.'
'Customers fear losing clothes more than they care about price, so visible tracking could be our strongest proof.'
quiz.explain: An insight explains what the observation means for the brand and points to a decision.

quiz.q: A consistency audit finds 7 of 10 touchpoints pass all checks. What is the score and the sensible next step?
options: 70%; fix easy high-visibility items such as bios and greetings first
70%; do nothing because it is above half
quiz.explain: 7 divided by 10 is 70%. Quick, visible fixes give the biggest improvement first.

quiz.q: A client says, 'We registered our name with CAC, so nobody can use it.' What is the most accurate response?
options: Correct, CAC registration is a trademark
CAC business name registration is not the same as a trademark; trademarks go through the Trademarks, Patents and Designs Registry, and a lawyer can advise
Names cannot be protected in Nigeria
quiz.explain: Business name registration and trademark registration are separate processes. Point the client to the right registry and a qualified lawyer.

modules.title: Consulting Practice: Discovery, Proposals and Portfolio
modules.overview: Learn to run discovery that finds the real problem, price and propose positioning work with clear scope, lead a team workshop, measure results honestly and plan your first paid project.

lessons.title: Client discovery: questions that find the real problem
objectives: Prepare a pre-call form and a 45-minute discovery call agenda
Use a question bank and the 'five whys' to move from symptoms to root causes
Recognise when the problem is not branding and say so honestly
Spot client red flags before you send a proposal

blocks.text: Clients usually arrive with a solution already in mind: "we need a new logo", "we need a rebrand", "we need to go viral". Discovery is your chance to understand the business before agreeing with them. Good discovery protects the client's money and your reputation, because the right diagnosis makes the work succeed.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people in a structured conversation across a table
blocks.caption: Discovery is a structured conversation that finds the real problem before any proposal is written.

blocks.text: Before the call

Send a short Google Form or WhatsApp list of questions a day before. It saves call time and shows how organised the client is. Six questions are enough: what the business sells, who buys most, what has changed recently, what result they want in six months, who makes the final decision, and the budget range they have in mind.
A 45-minute discovery call

items: Minutes 0 to 5: thank them, confirm the time, explain the purpose: to understand, not to sell.
Minutes 5 to 25: business and customers. Use the question bank below and take notes.
Minutes 25 to 35: competitors and what makes them different, in their own words.
Minutes 35 to 40: success. 'If this works, what will be different in six months?'
Minutes 40 to 45: next steps. Tell them when your proposal or recommendation will arrive.

head: Area
Questions to ask
rows: What result matters most this year? How will you know it worked?
Who are your best customers? Why do they come back? Who leaves, and why?
Which product or service makes the most profit? Which one do you secretly wish you could stop?
Who do customers compare you with? When do you lose a sale, who wins it?
What do you do every single time without fail? What sometimes goes wrong?
Who else must approve this? What has stopped past projects?

blocks.text: Listening matters more than asking. Let short silences sit, because owners often add the most useful detail after a pause. Write down their exact words, especially how they describe customers and competitors. At the end of each section, summarise back in one sentence, for example 'So your best customers are office admins who reorder when delivery is on time, is that right?' The client either confirms or corrects you, and both help.
The five whys
When a client names a symptom, ask "why" several times, gently, until you reach a cause you can act on. Five is a guide, not a rule; stop when the answer points to something specific.

blocks.title: Worked example: the cake shop that wanted a rebrand
blocks.context: For example, Chioma owns a cake shop in Enugu. She says sales of celebration cakes fell over six months and asks for a new logo and name.
steps: Why did sales fall? 'Fewer repeat orders from people who bought before.'
Why fewer repeat orders? 'Some customers complained.'
Why did they complain? Chioma checks her WhatsApp: 9 of the last 30 cake orders had complaints, and 7 of those 9 were about cakes arriving damaged.
Why were cakes damaged? 'We switched to cheaper, thinner boxes and a new dispatch rider.'
Why the switch? 'To save about 500 naira (approximate) per order.'
blocks.result: The root cause is delivery packaging, not the logo. 9 of 30 is 30% of orders with complaints, and 7 of 9, about 78% of complaints, are about damage. The honest recommendation: fix boxes and delivery first, then position the shop on 'arrives perfect' with a photo sent before dispatch. A new logo now would have cost money and changed nothing.

blocks.title: Symptom versus root cause
items: What the client says
What discovery found
blocks.caption: Discovery moves the conversation from the client's suggested solution to the cause that really drives results.

blocks.text: When the problem is not branding

Positioning cannot fix a poor product, a broken delivery process, prices far above what customers will pay, or a cash flow crisis. If discovery shows one of these, say it clearly and in writing. You can still offer help: a smaller project, a referral to someone better placed, or a positioning project once the operation is fixed. Clients remember honest advice and often come back.
Red flags to notice

items: No clear decision-maker, or a decision-maker who will not attend any meeting.
A deadline that leaves no time for research, for example 'launch on Friday'.
Expecting guaranteed sales numbers or 'going viral'.
Refusing to share basic facts such as price lists or customer feedback.
Pressure to start work before any deposit or written agreement.

blocks.title: Protect yourself and the client
blocks.text: Never ask clients for passwords, bank PINs or OTPs. If you need access to a social account, ask them to add you as a team member through the platform's settings. Keep client information confidential and store it only in the project folder.

takeaways: Clients bring solutions; discovery finds the real problem.
A pre-call form plus a 45-minute agenda keeps discovery focused.
The five whys move from symptom to an actionable cause.
If the problem is not branding, say so in writing and offer a fitting next step.

activity.title: Discovery pack
steps: Create a six-question pre-call form in Google Forms or as a WhatsApp message.
Write your 45-minute agenda and a question bank of at least twelve questions.
Run a discovery conversation with the owner of your course business (or role-play with a friend).
Apply the five whys to the main problem they describe.
Write a half-page discovery summary: symptom, root cause, whether branding can help, and recommended next step.
activity.evidence: Your pre-call form, question bank and the half-page discovery summary.

lessons.title: Pricing, proposals and scope control for positioning work
objectives: Package positioning work into three clear offers
Calculate a fee from your hours and minimum hourly rate, then check it against the value to the client
Write a proposal with deliverables, timeline, payment terms and scope limits
Handle extra requests with a written change request

blocks.text: Brand strategy is thinking work, so clients cannot see it the way they see a cake or a dress. Clear packages, clear prices and clear limits make the work easy to buy and protect you from endless extra requests.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A signed agreement with a pen
blocks.caption: A proposal with clear scope and payment terms is the foundation of a smooth project.

blocks.text: Three packages

head: Package
What is included
Typical time
rows: Discovery call, 2-hour workshop with the owner, positioning statement, messaging house
Everything in the Sprint plus customer interviews, competitor audit, perceptual map, route testing and a mini brand guideline
Monthly check of content and touchpoints against the guideline, one review call, quarterly consistency audit

blocks.text: From hours to a fee

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing the three packages
blocks.context: For example, Amaka is a marketing professional in Lagos building a brand strategy practice on the side. Her figures are illustrative and her prices approximate.
steps: Income goal: 600,000 naira a month from this work. Billable hours she can realistically sell: 60 a month.
Minimum hourly rate: 600,000 divided by 60 = 10,000 naira per hour.
Full Project: 30 hours x 10,000 = 300,000 naira. She adds 15% for meetings and revisions: 300,000 x 1.15 = 345,000. She rounds to 350,000 naira.
Sprint: 12 hours x 10,000 = 120,000. Plus 15% = 138,000. Rounded: 140,000 naira.
Retainer: 8 hours x 10,000 = 80,000 naira a month.
Value check for a client like Bisi from Module 1: if a clearer position adds 20,000 naira profit per tray on 4 trays a month, that is 80,000 naira a month, or 960,000 naira a year.
blocks.result: Amaka's fees cover her time, and the Full Project at 350,000 naira is well below the yearly value it could create for a client like Bisi. She explains the price using the value, not her hours.

blocks.title: Your rate is a floor, not the price
blocks.text: The hourly calculation tells you the lowest fee that keeps you in business. The final price also depends on the client's size and the value the work can create. A small trader and a mid-sized manufacturer should not pay the same for the same hours.

Keep a simple record of actual hours for every project, broken down by stage. After three projects, compare actual hours with your estimates. If research always takes 14 hours instead of 10, update your package hours and fees, rather than quietly working unpaid hours on every job.
The proposal

blocks.title: From enquiry to kickoff
items: Enquiry
Discovery call
Proposal within 3 days
Signed agreement and deposit
Kickoff meeting
blocks.caption: Work starts only after the agreement and deposit, never before.

items: **Our understanding**: the client's situation and goal in their own words from discovery.
**Approach**: the stages from Module 2, in plain language.
**Deliverables**: exactly what they receive, for example 'one positioning statement, one messaging house, a 6-page guideline'.
**Timeline**: dates for each check-in and the final handover.
**Investment**: the package price and what it includes. Offering two options (Sprint and Full Project) lets the client choose instead of saying no.
**Terms**: 50% deposit to start, 50% on delivery, payment by bank transfer or a Paystack payment link, and how long the offer is valid.
**Next step**: one clear action, such as 'reply YES and I will send the invoice'.

blocks.text: Presenting the price

Send the proposal, then offer a 20-minute call to walk through it, so the client hears your reasoning instead of jumping straight to the number. If they say it is too expensive, do not cut the price of the same work. Offer a smaller scope instead: the Sprint instead of the Full Project, fewer interviews, or the guideline later. Cutting price without cutting scope teaches the client that your first figure was not real. A retainer works best after a project, when the client has seen the value and wants help keeping the brand consistent month by month.
Scope control

Most project problems come from vague scope. Write limits into the proposal: the number of customer interviews (for example, eight), the number of positioning routes (three), revision rounds on the final document (two), and what is **not** included, such as logo design, website building, paid adverts or printing. When the client asks for more, send a short written change request with the extra hours, the fee and the new deadline, and wait for a 'yes' before doing it.

blocks.title: Payment safety
blocks.text: Confirm every payment in your own bank or Paystack app before starting work. Screenshots of transfers can be faked. Never share OTPs or PINs, and be wary of 'clients' who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference, a common scam pattern.

takeaways: Package thinking work into clear offers with visible deliverables.
Hourly rate = income goal divided by billable hours; it is your floor.
Explain price with the value to the client, not only your hours.
Write scope limits and use change requests for anything extra.

activity.title: Your packages and a proposal
steps: Set your income goal and realistic billable hours and calculate your minimum hourly rate.
Estimate hours for a Sprint and a Full Project and calculate fees with a 15% buffer.
Do a value check for one realistic client type.
Write a one to two page proposal for your course business using the seven sections.
Add a scope section listing four limits and three exclusions.
activity.evidence: Your pricing calculation sheet and the proposal document.

lessons.title: Case studies, leading workshops and your 90-day practice plan
objectives: Write an honest case study that shows your positioning process and results
Facilitate a two-hour positioning workshop with a business team
Track simple brand health measures after launch
Plan the next 90 days to win and deliver your first paid positioning project

blocks.text: Clients buy strategy from people they trust. Trust comes from showing your thinking, leading a room well and reporting results honestly. This lesson turns your course project into proof and gives you a plan to find paying work.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.alt: A portfolio of project cards laid out on a screen
blocks.caption: A small portfolio of honest case studies is the strongest sales tool for strategy work.

blocks.text: The case study

items: **Client and challenge**: who they are and what was wrong, in two or three sentences.
**What you did**: the research, insights and routes, with one image such as the perceptual map.
**The position**: the final statement and the messaging house.
**What changed**: only measured results, with dates, for example enquiries before and after.
**Client quote**: only with written permission, word for word.

blocks.title: Honesty rules for portfolios
blocks.text: Label practice projects as practice. Do not claim results you did not measure or that other factors caused. Hide customer names and numbers unless the client agrees in writing. One honest case study is worth more than five inflated ones.
Leading a positioning workshop

A workshop helps a team agree on the position together, so they own it. Keep it to two hours, with the owner and two to five key staff. You need sticky notes or a WhatsApp poll, markers, and your research summary.

head: Time
Activity
Output
rows: Goal of the session and ground rules
Present customer evidence: quotes, map, competitor grid
Everyone writes possible points of difference; group them; dot vote with 3 dots each
Draft a positioning statement for the top two differences in pairs
Agree what to test with customers and who does what

blocks.text: As facilitator you stay neutral, keep time, make sure quieter staff speak, and bring the conversation back to customer evidence when people argue from personal taste. Front-line staff such as riders and sales attendants often know customers best; invite them.

Dot voting is simple: each person gets three sticky dots, or three votes in a WhatsApp poll, and places them on the differences they believe customers value most. It gives quieter people an equal voice. End the workshop by reading the agreed actions aloud and sending them in writing the same day.
The handover presentation

When the project ends, present the strategy in about 45 minutes: the goal you agreed, what customers told you, the routes you tested and the results, the final position, and exactly how to use the guideline from tomorrow. Leave time for questions from staff. A week after handover, ask the client for a short written testimonial while the work is fresh, and ask permission to use it.
Measuring brand health after launch

blocks.title: Position, measure, refine
items: Launch the position
Track simple measures
Review every month
Refine messages, not the core
blocks.caption: Keep the core position steady for months, and adjust how it is expressed based on evidence.

blocks.text: Agree a few measures before launch so you can compare. Useful ones for small businesses: enquiries per week, the share of enquiries that mention the promise, conversion rate (orders divided by enquiries), average order value, number of discount requests, and repeat customers.

blocks.title: Worked example: three months after launch
blocks.context: For example, Tolu's laundry relaunched with its weekend work-shirt position. She logs WhatsApp enquiries and orders in a simple Google Sheet.
steps: Month before launch: 40 enquiries, 10 orders. Conversion = 10 divided by 40 = 25%.
Third month after launch: 45 enquiries, 15 orders. Conversion = 15 divided by 45 = 33%.
Average order before: 3,500 naira (5 shirts x 700). After: 4,900 naira (7 shirts x 700), because customers send all their work shirts at once.
Discount requests fell from 6 to 2 a month.
She notes other changes in the same period, such as a new estate opening nearby, so she does not credit everything to the brand.
blocks.result: Conversion rose from 25% to about 33% and average order value from 3,500 to 4,900 naira. The evidence supports the position, and Tolu has an honest result for a case study.

blocks.text: Your 90-day plan

head: Days
Focus
Target
rows: Finish your capstone and write it up as a case study
One complete case study and a one-page service sheet
Reach one client type, for example food vendors or salons in your city
One paid Sprint, one written testimonial, updated hour estimates

blocks.text: Leadership in this field also means continuing to learn. Read positioning classics such as Ries and Trout, follow good brand case studies, and review your own projects each quarter: what you would ask earlier, what took longer than planned, and which insights proved right.

takeaways: Case studies show your process and only honestly measured results.
A two-hour workshop helps a team own the position.
Track enquiries, conversion, order value and discount requests before and after.
A 90-day plan turns course work into a first paid project.

activity.title: Case study and 90-day plan
steps: Write a one-page case study of your course project using the five headings, labelled as practice if it is.
Plan a two-hour workshop agenda for your course business using the timing table.
Choose four brand health measures and record a 'before' number for each.
Write your 90-day plan with targets for each 30-day block.
Share the case study with one trusted person and ask for one improvement.
activity.evidence: Your case study, workshop agenda, baseline measures and 90-day plan.

quiz.q: A client asks for a new logo because sales fell. Discovery shows 70% of complaints are about late delivery. What should you recommend?
options: Fix delivery first, then position on reliability once it is true
Run discounts to win customers back
quiz.explain: The root cause is operational. Branding cannot fix it, and promising reliability before fixing delivery would break trust.

quiz.q: Your income goal is 450,000 naira a month and you can sell 45 billable hours. What is your minimum hourly rate?
A project needs 20 hours at 10,000 naira per hour plus a 15% buffer. What is the fee before rounding?
Halfway through, a client asks you to also design their Instagram posts, which your proposal excluded. What is the professional response?
options: Do it free to keep them happy
Send a written change request with the extra hours, fee and new deadline, and wait for approval
Quietly reduce the quality of the main work to make time
quiz.explain: Change requests keep the relationship fair and protect the agreed scope.

quiz.q: Enquiries rose from 50 to 60 and orders from 10 to 18 after launch. What happened to conversion?
quiz.explain: Before: 10 divided by 50 = 20%. After: 18 divided by 60 = 30%.

quiz.q: In a positioning workshop, two managers argue from personal taste about which difference to choose. What should the facilitator do?
options: Let the most senior person decide immediately
Bring the discussion back to the customer evidence and use dot voting
quiz.explain: The facilitator stays neutral and anchors decisions in customer evidence, then uses a fair method to choose.

finalQuiz.q: What is the difference between brand identity and brand position?
options: Identity is the tools you control (name, logo, colours); position is the place you choose to own in the customer's mind
Identity is for big companies; position is for small ones
Position is the logo; identity is the price
finalQuiz.explain: Identity expresses the position. A new logo without a chosen position changes how you look, not what you stand for.

finalQuiz.q: Which pair names the two things strong positioning must balance within a frame of reference?
options: Points of parity and points of difference
finalQuiz.explain: Parity gets the brand considered and difference gets it chosen, as Keller, Sternthal and Tybout describe.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the best target segment description for positioning?
options: Working parents in Gwarinpa whose children are preparing for BECE or WAEC
finalQuiz.explain: It describes a specific group, situation and need that the business can reach and serve.

finalQuiz.q: A segment scores size 3, pay 4, reach 4, fit 2 with weights 30%, 30%, 25%, 15%. What is the score?
Which question best uncovers the 'job' a customer hires a product to do?
options: 'What was happening the last time you bought this, and what else did you consider?'
'How much would you pay in future?'
finalQuiz.explain: Past behaviour in a real situation reveals the progress the customer wanted to make.

finalQuiz.q: How should you choose the two axes of a perceptual map?
options: From what customers said matters in interviews and reviews
finalQuiz.explain: Axes must reflect what customers actually use to choose, or the gaps you find will be meaningless.

finalQuiz.q: In a route test, 9 of 15 customers chose Route A. Which report is accurate?
options: '60% of the market wants Route A'
'9 of the 15 customers we spoke to, 60%, chose Route A'
finalQuiz.explain: 9 divided by 15 is 60%. Report the real sample size and do not generalise to the whole market.

finalQuiz.q: What sits on the 'roof' of a messaging house?
options: The brand promise in one line
finalQuiz.explain: The roof is the promise; the pillars support it and the foundation holds the proof.

finalQuiz.q: A brand guideline audit finds the Instagram bio still describes the old 'all services' offer. What should happen?
options: Ignore it, bios do not matter
Rewrite the bio to state the new promise, a quick high-visibility fix
finalQuiz.explain: Bios are seen often and cost nothing to fix, so they come first in the action list.

finalQuiz.q: During discovery, which is a red flag?
options: The owner shares price lists and customer feedback
The client wants work started today with no deposit or written agreement
The client asks how long the project will take
finalQuiz.explain: Starting without an agreement or deposit exposes you to unpaid work and unclear scope.

finalQuiz.q: Income goal 800,000 naira a month, 50 billable hours. A Sprint takes 12 hours plus a 15% buffer. What is the Sprint fee before rounding?
Three months after launch, conversion improved but a new estate also opened nearby. How should the case study report this?
options: Credit the whole improvement to the new brand
Report the measured change and mention the other factor honestly
Double the numbers to impress clients
finalQuiz.explain: Honest case studies report measured results and note other factors that may have contributed.

capstone.title: Brand Positioning Strategy Package
capstone.brief: Produce a complete positioning package for a real or practice business: a researched positioning statement, a mini brand guideline that turns it into everyday messaging, and a priced proposal and 90-day plan for offering positioning work to a specific client type.
steps: Choose the business and write a one-page brief with goal, decision-maker and scope.
Score three or more segments and choose a primary target.
Complete at least five customer interviews, a review mining sheet, a competitor audit grid and a perceptual map.
Write five insights and two or three positioning routes, then test them with at least six target customers.
